A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SCQL framework and StaCQ algorithm. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite reorganization and added material.

before.justification: v1 reports original maze-navigation outcomes and D4RL evaluations of StaCQ and its one-step variant, including five-seed results in Table 1.

after.justification: v2 retains original maze and D4RL results and adds controlled comparisons, reachability ablations, and training curves in Appendices E–G.

M1.justification: The specified StaCQ update now uses a target actor in the critic target and adds its soft update in Algorithm 1. The main actor loss changes from positive to negative lambda times Q, correcting its inconsistency with the stated maximization objective. These are local specification changes; the PDFs do not establish corresponding code changes.

E1.justification: The same 18 D4RL datasets and original maze example remain. Appendix H adds an idealized sparse-maze scenario with gaps that prevent one-step stitching but permit paths through non-dataset intermediate states. This modestly extends the illustrative scenario coverage, without adding a benchmark domain.

E2.justification: The benchmark comparator set remains BC, BCQ, TD3+BC, IQL, MBTS, Diffuser, and RAMBO. Appendix E retests existing comparators with different tuning and critic-count settings; POR is newly discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: Appendix E adds controlled designs using a fixed StaCQ hyperparameter across locomotion datasets and environment-tuned TD3+BC with four critics. Appendix F systematically varies three reachability norms and four thresholds. These substantially expand evaluation controls, while Appendix C retains the original benchmark settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds tuning and critic-count controls, reachability sensitivity tests on Walker2d-Medium and MediumExpert, learning curves across the benchmark datasets, and a two-step maze case study. These investigate confounding, failure conditions, training behavior, and stitching limitations that v1 did not analyze.

E5.justification: Both versions retain five-seed evaluation with 10 locomotion or 100 Antmaze trajectories. v2 explicitly identifies standard deviations in the new table captions and introduces shaded standard-deviation bands across training; v1's Table 1 leaves its plus/minus statistic unnamed. No increased seed count or formal significance testing is established.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises several StaCQ results, including Hopper-Random from 9.1 ± 0.9 to 17.5 ± 12.8 and the Antmaze total from 309.6 to 319.8; its baseline and OneStep scores remain unchanged. New controlled and sensitivity results substantially expand the evidence: Table 3 reports Walker2d-MediumExpert falling from 116.2 ± 1.5 to 6.7 ± 12.4 when the L-infinity threshold increases from 0.1 to 0.5. The original score revisions are not explained as same-procedure gains.

T1.justification: Appendix H expands v1's brief multi-step suggestion into a dataset-anchored two-step reachability definition and tentative value-update and policy-extraction equations. Section 7 also proposes a stochastic reachability definition. The original convergence assumptions, results, and proofs remain substantially intact; no completed multi-step convergence proof is added.

C1.justification: Both versions claim a less restrictive state-constrained framework, convergence and policy dominance under stated assumptions, and strong StaCQ benchmark performance. Although v2's abstract explicitly says state-of-the-art, v1 already makes that claim in its discussion. Multi-step learning remains a prospective extension.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands applicability and failure discussions: deterministic versus stochastic environments, false reachability estimates at loose thresholds, tuning and critic-count fairness, and accumulated model error and computational costs for multi-step extensions. These qualify and explain the results beyond v1's largely forward-looking discussion.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code-repository link and newly states the original maze's reward values, learning rate, discount, and convergence duration. Appendix G discloses evaluation every 5,000 training steps. Existing architecture, normalization, hyperparameter, hardware, and runtime details in Appendices B–D are largely unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of POR and its relationship to IQL and state-constrained learning, citing Xu et al. (2022). It also adds Jin et al. (2021) and Shi et al. (2022) in the theoretical discussion. The broader positioning against batch-constrained and model-based approaches remains.

P1.justification: Related work moves from Section 2 to Section 5, QA/QS terminology becomes QSA/QSS, and substantial portions of the introduction, related work, experimental discussion, and conclusion are rewritten. This is extensive narrative revision beyond adding the new scientific material.

P2.justification: v2 adds a reachability schematic, two experimental tables, a six-panel learning-curve figure, and a second maze comparison. The original maze figure is retained and renumbered. Journal formatting also changes typography, table spacing, headers, and algorithm placement throughout.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important weaknesses in v1's empirical support: Appendix E controls tuning and critic-count differences, while Appendix F tests the central reachability choice and exposes severe failures. Learning curves, clearer applicability limits, and added reproducibility information further strengthen the paper. Reporting remains imperfect, including conflicting per-environment versus per-dataset wording in Table 2, but this limited ambiguity does not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and transparency.
